items.prompt: What is a decision matrix used for?

options.label: Scoring options against weighted criteria
Recording which attendees agreed or objected in a meeting
Predicting future sales by extending past trends
Listing project tasks in order of their due dates

rubric: A decision matrix rates each option on stated criteria, often with weights, so options can be compared.
Distractors describe forecasting, task lists and minutes, which are different tools.

items.prompt: How is expected value calculated?

options.label: The plain average of outcomes, ignoring odds
The value of the single most likely outcome, ignoring the rest
The best outcome minus the worst outcome
Each outcome's value times its probability, summed

rubric: Expected value is the sum of value times probability across all outcomes.
Distractors ignore probabilities or use only one outcome.

items.prompt: In decision making, what is a 'sunk cost'?

options.label: Money held in reserve to cover unexpected problems or delays
Money or effort already spent that cannot be recovered
The extra one-off cost of switching to a new supplier
The price of the cheapest option available on the market

rubric: A sunk cost is already spent and cannot be recovered whatever you choose next.
Distractors confuse it with contingency funds, minimum price or switching costs.

items.prompt: What is the usual first step in a structured decision process?

options.label: Ask everyone affected to vote on the final choice
Give every available option a score out of ten
Pick the option that feels most right to you
Define the decision and what you want to achieve

rubric: You must frame the decision and objective before generating or scoring options.
Distractors jump to choosing, scoring or voting before the choice is framed.

items.prompt: Which term names choosing the first option that meets your minimum requirements, rather than searching for the best one?

options.label: Satisficing
Maximising
Hedging
Anchoring

rubric: Satisficing means accepting the first option that is good enough.
Maximising is searching for the best; anchoring and hedging are different ideas.

items.prompt: Which of these are parts of a decision matrix? Select all that apply.

options.label: A coin flip to settle every close result
A record of who proposed each option
Criteria used to judge them
Scores for each option on each criterion
A list of options

rubric: A matrix needs options, criteria and scores, often plus weights.
Coin flips and proposer records are not components of the method.

items.prompt: Before launching a new service, a manager asks the team to imagine it is a year later and the launch has failed. Each person writes down the reasons it might have failed. What is this technique called?

options.label: A pre-mortem
A post-implementation review
A decision tree
A SWOT analysis

rubric: A pre-mortem imagines failure in advance to surface risks before committing.
A post-implementation review happens after the fact; SWOT and decision trees work differently.

items.prompt: Why do we assign weights to criteria in a decision matrix?

options.label: They show some criteria matter more, so important ones count for more in the total
They make every criterion count equally so that no single factor dominates the total
They remove the need to score each option by ranking the criteria alone
They guarantee that the top-scoring option will succeed once it is chosen

rubric: Weights reflect relative importance so major criteria influence the total more.
Distractors claim equal counting, no scoring, or guaranteed success, all misreading weights.

items.prompt: A choice has an expected value of 30 dollars. What does this mean?

options.label: The amount you will receive on the next single try
The smallest amount you could possibly receive
The average result per decision over many repeats
The most likely single outcome of any one attempt

rubric: Expected value is a long-run average, not a guarantee for one try.
Distractors treat it as a single-try result, a minimum or a mode.

items.prompt: Why does a pre-mortem help a team make a better decision?

options.label: It proves the plan will succeed whenever the team can list only a few problems
It assigns blame early so that each owner feels accountable for the outcome
It replaces the need for a plan once the main risks have all been found
It lets people voice doubts by assuming failure, countering overconfidence

rubric: Assuming failure frees people to raise concerns and reduces overconfidence.
Distractors treat it as proof, a plan substitute or a blame exercise.

items.prompt: Choosing between two jobs when you cannot know how the industry will change is a decision made under what condition?

options.label: Uncertainty
Delegation
Compulsion
Certainty

rubric: When outcomes depend on unknown future events, the decision is made under uncertainty.
Certainty would mean outcomes are known; the others are not decision conditions.

items.prompt: Why is it a mistake to continue a failing project mainly because of the money already spent on it?

options.label: Past spending shows the project is close to paying off, so quitting now would waste the chance of a return
That money is gone whichever option you pick, so it should not decide the choice
Stopping is always better than continuing once costs have started to pile up past the original budget
Money already spent should be counted again as a cost of stopping, so it tilts the comparison toward continuing

rubric: Sunk costs are identical across options, so only future costs and benefits should count.
Distractors invert the logic or claim stopping is always better.

items.prompt: Which are good reasons to use a structured method such as a decision matrix instead of relying only on gut feeling? Select all that apply.

options.label: It guarantees a good outcome every time
It reduces the pull of a single bias or favourite option
It removes any need to judge how important criteria are
It helps compare all options on the same criteria
It makes the reasoning visible so others can check it

rubric: Structure makes reasoning transparent, consistent and less bias-prone.
It cannot guarantee outcomes or remove judgement about weights.

items.prompt: A team scores three suppliers in a matrix where cost has a 50% weight. Supplier B is weak on cost but strong on quality and support, and ranks third. A colleague argues that cost should matter less, and the team lowers its weight to 20%. What is the most likely effect?

options.label: All suppliers' totals rise by the same amount, so the ranking stays the same
Supplier B moves up because its strong scores count for more
Supplier B stays third because the raw scores are fixed and only the totals change
Nothing changes because scores matter more than weights in a matrix

rubric: Lowering cost's weight shifts importance to quality and support, where B is strong.
Distractors assume weights don't affect totals or that all totals move equally.

items.prompt: In a decision matrix, what is the purpose of giving criteria different weights?

options.label: They guarantee the result is objective and free of personal bias
They let the scorer skip rating options on the lower-weighted criteria
They show that some criteria matter more than others
They keep one high score on a single criterion from dominating the total

rubric: Weights express how much each criterion matters to the decider.
Weights do not remove bias or replace listing options; the strongest distractor overstates objectivity.

items.prompt: What does the expected value of a choice tell you?

options.label: The worst outcome you would face, which sets how much risk to take
The probability-weighted average of outcomes if repeated many times
The best outcome the choice could produce, adjusted for its cost
The most likely single outcome, which is the one to plan around

rubric: Expected value is the average of outcomes weighted by their probabilities.
Distractors confuse it with the most likely, best-case or worst-case outcome.

items.prompt: What is a pre-mortem?

options.label: Imagining the plan has already failed, then working out why
Ranking team members by how likely they are to cause a delay
Estimating the plan's chance of success as a single percentage
Reviewing a finished project to record what went wrong afterwards

rubric: A pre-mortem assumes failure in advance to surface risks while the plan can still change.
A post-project review is a post-mortem, which is the most tempting distractor.

items.prompt: Why should sunk costs be left out when choosing what to do next?

options.label: They are usually too small to change the total cost of any option, so they rarely matter
They are the same whichever option you pick, so they can't separate the options
They only count when the money was originally spent by someone else on your behalf
They are hard to measure accurately, so they distort the scores in a comparison

rubric: Sunk costs cannot be recovered under any option, so they do not help distinguish options.
Distractors give size or measurement reasons rather than the real one.

items.prompt: A manager frames a problem as 'Should we fire our current supplier, yes or no?' What is the main risk of this framing?

options.label: It opens up too many options to compare with any structured method
It makes the decision depend on probabilities that can't be known in advance
It forces the manager to treat all criteria as equally important when scoring
It offers only two options and may hide others, like renegotiating

rubric: A yes/no frame narrows the option set and can hide alternatives.
The other options misdescribe what a narrow frame does.

items.prompt: Which of these are genuine benefits of running a pre-mortem before launching a plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: It makes a decision matrix unnecessary for the choice
It proves the plan will succeed if no problems are listed
It surfaces risks while the plan can still be changed
It gives team members permission to voice doubts about the plan

rubric: Pre-mortems make dissent safe and expose risks early.
They do not prove success or replace other methods; a short list of risks can reflect poor imagination.

items.prompt: A team must choose between two expensive commercial software tools and spends a week comparing them. A new colleague asks whether a free open-source tool could meet their needs, and nobody had considered it. What does this situation best illustrate?

options.label: The criteria weights were set wrongly, so the scoring of the two tools was misleading
The team gave too little weight to the cost of delay while it compared the tools
The team needed more precise probabilities for each tool's chance of success
Options were framed too narrowly; widening the set can reveal better choices

rubric: The team limited itself to two options; broadening the option set can improve the decision.
Weights and probabilities were not the problem here.

items.prompt: There is a 25% chance of an 8000 loss, otherwise no loss. Insurance costs a certain 2500. Judging on expected money only, what is the best choice?

options.label: Buy insurance: the expected loss is 6000, more than the premium
Skip insurance: the expected loss is 2000, less than the premium
Buy insurance: the expected loss is 8000, more than the premium
Skip insurance: the expected loss is 2500, equal to the premium

rubric: Expected loss is 0.25 x 8000 = 2000, below the 2500 premium.
Distractors use the wrong probability (0.75) or ignore probability altogether.

items.prompt: Weights: price 3, quality 5, speed 2. Option A scores 4, 3, 5 on price, quality, speed. Option B scores 2, 5, 4. Which option wins on weighted total?

options.label: A wins, 12 to 11
B wins, 39 to 37
Tie, 38 each
A wins, 37 to 36

rubric: Choosing A comes from adding raw scores and ignoring the weights.

items.prompt: You have defined the decision, listed three options and chosen your criteria, but nothing is scored. Which step comes next in building the matrix?

options.label: Total each option's score and choose the highest
Drop any option that doesn't clearly win on the first criterion
Decide the weights before scoring, so preferences don't bias them
Score each option first, then set weights that favour the front-runner

rubric: Setting weights before scoring keeps the weights from being bent to favour a preferred option.
Totalling needs scores and weights first; adjusting weights afterwards defeats the method.

items.prompt: Your team is about to launch a new service. Which instruction correctly sets up a pre-mortem?

options.label: Ask everyone to describe the most likely successful outcome and list the steps that would get the team there
Hold a review after launch so the team can assign blame for each problem and agree on fixes
Say it is six months after launch and it failed; each person lists reasons why
Ask each person to argue why the launch will definitely succeed, then list objections to those arguments

rubric: A pre-mortem states failure as fact and asks for causes.
The other prompts ask for success reasons, blame or likely success, none of which surface risks.

items.prompt: You paid a non-refundable 60 for a concert ticket but feel unwell on the day. Which reasoning applies the sunk cost principle correctly?

options.label: Weigh the enjoyment of the show against resting, ignoring the price
Go, because staying home would waste the money and make the loss certain
Go only if you could resell the ticket for at least what you paid for it
Stay home, because the ticket money is lost and going adds more cost

rubric: The 60 is gone either way, so compare only future enjoyment and cost.
The other options let the past payment drive the choice in one direction or another.

items.prompt: You want to compare two options by expected value. Which steps would you take? Select all that apply.

options.label: Average each option's outcomes without using probabilities
Check that each option's probabilities add up to 100%
Pick the option with the largest single possible payoff
Multiply each outcome by its probability and add the results
List each option's possible outcomes with their probabilities

rubric: Expected value needs outcomes, valid probabilities and a weighted sum.
Choosing the largest payoff or taking a plain average ignores probability.

items.prompt: A team scores three suppliers from 1 to 5 on cost, quality and delivery. They gave the most expensive supplier a 5 on cost because it has the highest cost figure, and the weighted totals now favour it. The team lead notices the mistake. What should the team do?

options.label: Keep the scores but double the weight of quality to offset the cost error in the totals
Reduce the weight on cost to zero so the error no longer matters in the totals
Remove cost as a criterion since it can't share a 1 to 5 scale with the others
Rescore cost so the cheapest supplier gets 5, then recompute the weighted totals

rubric: Higher scores must mean better, so cost has to be scored in reverse before weighting.
The other fixes hide the error instead of correcting the scoring direction.

items.prompt: An option gives a 40% chance of gaining 500 and a 60% chance of losing 100. What is its expected value?
rubric: Distractor 200 ignores the loss branch, a common slip of counting only the gain.

items.prompt: Criteria weights are cost 3 and quality 2. Option A scores cost 4 and quality 5; Option B scores cost 5 and quality 3 (higher is better). Which option leads on weighted score?

options.label: A, with 9 against 8 for B
A, with 22 against 21 for B
B, with 21 against 22 for A
B, with 25 against 22 for A, since cost carries the larger weight

rubric: A = 3x4 + 2x5 = 22; B = 3x5 + 2x3 = 21, so A leads.
Options 3 and 4 use unweighted sums, and option 1 reverses the totals.

items.prompt: A team has just been told to imagine that their project failed a year from now. Following the pre-mortem method, what should they do next?

options.label: Each person drafts a success story for the project, then the group picks the likeliest one as the target to plan around
The leader presents the plan again in full detail, then the group rates how confident each member feels about it
Each person privately lists reasons for the failure, then the group merges them and plans responses
Vote on whether to go ahead with the plan, then record any objections raised by those who disagree with the result

rubric: A pre-mortem collects independent failure reasons, then turns them into mitigations.
Other options turn it into a vote, a success story or a confidence poll, which does not surface risks.

items.prompt: Launching a feature costs 50. There is a 30% chance it returns 300 and a 70% chance it returns nothing. What is the expected net value of launching?
rubric: Expected return is 0.3 x 300 = 90; subtract the 50 cost to get 40.
Distractor 90 forgets the cost; -50 assumes failure.

items.prompt: A project has already cost 200k. Finishing needs another 100k and is expected to return 80k. Applying sound decision rules, what should you do?

options.label: Stop, because the project has already lost 200k and must not be allowed to lose any more money
Stop, because the extra 100k costs more than the 80k it is expected to return
Continue, because stopping would waste the 200k already spent on the project and lock in that loss
Continue, because 100k more is a small step beside the 200k already spent

rubric: Only future costs and returns matter: 100k to gain 80k is a loss, so stop.
Continue options reflect the sunk-cost fallacy.

items.prompt: You are building a weighted decision matrix to choose a vendor. Which steps are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Score every option on the same scale for each criterion
Multiply each score by its criterion weight and add the results
Adjust the weights after seeing totals until the favoured option wins
Drop any criterion on which the options differ widely
Agree the criteria and their weights before scoring any option

rubric: A sound matrix fixes criteria and weights first, uses a common scale, and sums weighted scores.
Tuning weights to a favourite or dropping discriminating criteria defeats the method.

items.prompt: Maya compares two job offers with a weighted matrix. Weights: salary 5, growth 3, commute 2. Offer X scores salary 4, growth 3, commute 5. Offer Y scores salary 5, growth 4, commute 2 (higher is better). Which result should she report?

options.label: Offer X, with 39 against 35 for Offer Y
Offer Y, with 41 against 39 for Offer X
A tie at 40 each, since the differences in salary and commute cancel out
Offer X, because its unweighted scores total 12 against 11 for Offer Y

rubric: Unweighted totals ignore the weights, and the other options contain arithmetic errors.

items.prompt: A team's matrix scores Option A at 84 and Option B at 82. Changing one weight by 5 percent flips the ranking. What is the soundest conclusion?

options.label: Option A wins, because the original weights were the ones the team formally agreed on before scoring
The options are effectively tied on these criteria, so other evidence should decide
The matrix is useless, because any result that can flip with small changes should be discarded
Option B wins, because the weights that produced the flip were set later and are likely more accurate

rubric: A small weight change flipping the order shows sensitivity: the gap is within the uncertainty of the weights.
Other options pick a winner arbitrarily or throw away the analysis.

items.prompt: An analyst's decision tree for one option has three outcomes with probabilities 50%, 40% and 30%, and reports an expected value of 180. What is the first problem to fix?

options.label: The payoffs must be discounted, since EV is always wrong without the time value of money
The 50% branch should be dropped, since the largest probability dominates the result
The probabilities total 120%, so the EV is inflated and the estimates must be revised
The tree should have only two outcomes, since three branches make EV unreliable

rubric: Branch probabilities must sum to 100%; at 120% every EV computed from them is overstated.
Other options invent rules that do not address the inconsistency.

items.prompt: A pre-mortem on a product launch, run with six engineers, produced 15 failure reasons, all technical. What is the most likely cause of this gap?

options.label: Pre-mortems surface only technical risks, so the method suits engineering projects alone
Fifteen reasons is too many, so the group naturally narrowed to the technical ones
Engineers are weak at imagining failure, so the manager should list the risks instead
The participants share one background, so market, legal and customer risks went unimagined

rubric: A homogeneous group tends to generate risks from its own viewpoint; adding other functions widens coverage.
Other options blame the method, the count or the people rather than the group mix.

items.prompt: Option A pays 100 for certain. Option B has a 90% chance of paying 150 and a 10% chance of losing 100, which the firm could not survive. B's EV is 125. Why can ranking by EV alone mislead here?

options.label: A 10% chance is negligible, so EV overstates the danger and B should clearly be chosen
EV averages over many repeats, but the firm faces a one-off loss it cannot survive
EV overweights the 10% loss, since probability weighting exaggerates how bad rare outcomes are
EV only works for certain outcomes, so a gamble like B cannot be evaluated with it

rubric: EV assumes repeated plays; with a ruinous outcome, survival matters more than the average.
Other options misdescribe what EV does.

items.prompt: Priya picked a supplier after comparing three bids, checking references and testing samples. The supplier then failed because of a rare fire, and a colleague calls the decision bad. What is the best analysis?

options.label: A sound process usually produces good results, so a hidden error probably exists somewhere in it
Judge the process and information available then; the fire was chance outside the evidence
Results are the fairest measure of a decision, so a failed supplier means a bad decision
The failure suggests a key risk was missed, so the process must have been flawed in some way

rubric: Decision quality should be separated from outcome quality; a sound process can meet bad luck.
Other options commit the 'resulting' error.

items.prompt: A decision matrix for choosing a supplier is giving odd results. Which features would distort it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Both 'unit cost' and 'total price' are listed as separate weighted criteria
A low weight is given to a criterion that matters little
Weights were agreed before scoring and sum to 100%
One criterion is scored 1-10 and another 1-100, then they are added without rescaling
A must-have requirement is just one weighted score, so a failing option can still win

rubric: Double counting, mixed scales and treating hard constraints as weights all distort totals.
Agreed weights and low weights for minor criteria are normal practice.

items.prompt: A manager funds launches using expected value. The team rates every launch 90% likely to hit target, yet past records show only 60% of launches did. EV rankings keep favouring launches that then disappoint. What is the best diagnosis and fix?

options.label: Probabilities are unreliable in principle, so drop EV and rank launches by cost alone, which is easier to measure
The EV method is flawed, so replace it with the judgment of the most senior member, who has seen the most launches
The team is overconfident, so pull estimates toward the 60% base rate and track results
The team is right to be optimistic, since past launches differ from these, so keep the 90% estimates and re-run EV

rubric: Persistent gaps between stated and historical success point to overconfidence; base rates and feedback recalibrate estimates.
Other options abandon the method or dismiss the evidence.

items.prompt: A team's weighted decision matrix scores Vendor A at 7.42 and Vendor B at 7.31. Shifting a single weight by five percentage points reverses the ranking. What does this most strongly indicate?

options.label: The weights were chosen badly, so the team should keep adjusting them until a stable winner finally appears
Vendor A is clearly superior, because it led under the original weights that the whole team had agreed on
The scoring method is invalid, so the matrix should be discarded and the choice made on gut feel
The vendors are effectively tied on this model, so the result hinges on the weights and needs a sensitivity check

rubric: A tiny weight change flipping a narrow gap shows the options are close, so a sensitivity check is the right response.
Distractors treat the flip as proof the method is useless, or as licence to keep tuning weights until a favoured result emerges.

items.prompt: A manager approves a one-off bet with expected value +$80k: 30% chance of +$500k and 70% chance of -$100k. The firm's cash reserve is $60k, and a $100k loss would force it to close. What does the EV figure fail to capture?

options.label: The EV is miscalculated, because the probabilities should be weighted by the size of each gain or loss
Opportunity cost, because EV only compares an option against doing nothing and never against other uses of money
Probability uncertainty, because EV cannot be used when any outcome has a probability below 50 percent
Ruin risk: one unrecoverable loss means long-run averaging never happens, so EV overstates the bet's worth

rubric: EV assumes repeated bets can average out; a single loss that ends the firm breaks that assumption.
Distractors misstate how EV is computed or when it can be used.

items.prompt: Why does a pre-mortem usually surface more risks than simply asking a team, 'What could go wrong?'

options.label: Picturing the failure as already happened makes explaining it easier and gives dissenters permission to speak
It assigns blame in advance, so each risk owner becomes personally accountable for preventing their own named failure
It makes the team pick the single most likely cause of failure, so that all effort goes to that one risk
It requires probability estimates for every risk, which stops vague worries from being raised in the meeting

rubric: Prospective hindsight lowers the social cost of voicing doubts and counters overconfidence and groupthink.
Distractors describe accountability, quantification or narrowing, none of which is the mechanism of a pre-mortem.

items.prompt: A matrix for choosing a laptop fleet uses four criteria, each weighted 25: purchase price, total cost over three years, performance, and battery life. Which analysis best identifies the main weakness?

options.label: Equal weights are always invalid, so every criterion must carry a different weight for the matrix to be credible
Performance and battery life are both technical, so they should be merged into one criterion before scoring
Price and total cost overlap, so cost effectively carries around 50 percent of the weight, likely more than intended
Four criteria are too few, since a sound matrix needs at least seven to avoid bias in the final ranking

rubric: Purchase price is part of total cost, so the two criteria double count cost and inflate its real weight.
Distractors apply invented rules about equal weights, merging criteria or minimum criteria counts.

items.prompt: In a project review, which statement is the clearest example of sunk-cost reasoning?

options.label: Our remaining budget would return more per dollar on the other project, so we should move it there.
We've put 18 months into this system, so switching to the cheaper vendor now would make that effort pointless.
If we stop now, we lose the chance to resell the equipment at full value next year, which exceeds the cost to finish.
Finishing needs another $150k and returns about $100k, so we should stop here even though we have spent $400k.

rubric: Justifying continuation by past spending that cannot be recovered is sunk-cost reasoning.
The other options all compare future costs and benefits, which is sound.

items.prompt: A team reviews a decision that turned out badly even though the analysis was careful. Which observations support the view that the decision was still reasonable? Select all that apply.

options.label: The bad outcome was given a low but nonzero probability when the choice was made
The team used the information available at the time and weighed it explicitly
A different option would have turned out better with hindsight
The bad outcome occurred, which shows the probabilities the team used were wrong

rubric: Decision quality is judged by the process and information at the time, not by one outcome.
Distractors confuse a single outcome or hindsight with proof of poor reasoning.

items.prompt: A hiring panel agrees to score three finalists on five criteria. After the interviews, the totals put Candidate C, a panel member's former colleague, in second place. Members then raise the weight on 'culture fit' from 10 to 25 percent, and C moves to first. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: Weights were changed after the scores were known, so the matrix is rationalising a favourite; fix weights beforehand
Culture fit was underweighted at first, so the revision corrects an honest error and improves the validity of the final ranking
The first totals were too close to separate the finalists, so the panel should average the members' ratings once more and then rank
The matrix is unreliable for hiring decisions, so the panel should drop scoring and switch to an open unstructured discussion

rubric: Changing weights after seeing results lets preference drive the outcome; weights must be set before scoring.
Distractors excuse the change as a correction or blame the tool rather than the process.

items.prompt: A firm wants to maximise expected profit but must avoid any possible loss above $100k. A: certain +$50k. B: 80% +$100k, 20% -$400k. C: 90% +$80k, 10% -$150k. D: 60% +$90k, 40% -$20k. Which option is best?

options.label: Option D
Option A
Option B
Option C

rubric: B and C breach the loss cap; A has EV $50k and D has EV $46k, so A is best among feasible options.
Choosing C ignores the cap despite its highest EV of $57k.

items.prompt: A choice is easily reversible within a week, costs under $200 to undo, and must be made by end of day. Judged on speed and proportionate effort, which approach is best?

options.label: Build a full weighted matrix with sensitivity analysis, so the choice stays defensible if anyone questions it later
Pick a good-enough option using a quick heuristic, then review the result after a week and reverse if needed
Run a department-wide pre-mortem first, since any failure of the choice would reflect on the whole team
Delay until more data arrives, since even reversible choices deserve complete information before anyone commits

rubric: For cheap, reversible choices under time pressure, a fast good-enough decision plus review is proportionate.
Distractors apply high-stakes methods or delay to a low-stakes decision.

items.prompt: An EV analysis for a product launch uses a single 60% success estimate from the project sponsor. The aim is to reduce bias and show how much the decision depends on that number. Which improvement best meets both aims?

options.label: Gather independent estimates from several people, use a range, and test whether the decision changes across it
Replace the 60% with the industry average success rate and then treat that figure as a known certainty
Drop probabilities entirely and rank options on best-case payoff, which avoids any false sense of precision
Ask the sponsor to justify the 60% in more detail, then keep it as the base case for the analysis

rubric: Independent estimates reduce bias, and testing the range shows how sensitive the decision is.
Distractors keep a single point estimate or discard probability altogether.

items.prompt: Launching pays +$200k with probability 0.5 and -$80k with probability 0.5; not launching pays $0. A market study costing $50k would give information about the outcome. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.label: Buy it: launching already has an EV of $60k, which comfortably exceeds the $50k cost of the study
Don't buy it: even perfect information is worth only $40k over the current EV, less than the $50k cost
Buy it: the study removes the 50 percent chance of a loss, and that is worth $100k to the firm
Don't buy it: the study is imperfect, so its value is zero because the launch EV is already positive

rubric: With perfect information the firm launches only on wins: EV $100k versus $60k now, so the value of information is at most $40k.
Distractors confuse the launch EV with the study's value or ignore that imperfect information can still have value.

items.prompt: A pre-mortem finds Risk X (50% likely, costs $10k) and Risk Y (0.1% likely, costs $5M and would end the company). The budget covers one mitigation. The criteria are to protect survival first, then minimise expected loss. Which is best?

options.label: Mitigate Y, because it threatens survival and its expected loss ($5k) equals X's
Mitigate X, because a 50 percent risk is far more likely to actually occur than a rare one, so it will almost surely cost money
Mitigate neither until the probability of Y can be measured much more precisely by the team, since a 0.1% estimate is unreliable
Mitigate X, because the expected losses are equal and X is easier to verify afterwards, which makes the spending easier to justify

rubric: Expected losses tie at $5k each, so the survival criterion decides in favour of Y.
Distractors rely on likelihood alone or postpone action despite the stated criteria.

items.prompt: A team ranks suppliers with a weighted-sum matrix in which 'meets legal compliance' is one criterion weighted 15%. A non-compliant supplier scores highest elsewhere and ranks first. Which critiques are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Weighted sums are compensatory, so strong scores elsewhere can offset a failure that should disqualify
Compliance should be a pass/fail screen applied before scoring the remaining criteria
The fix is to raise the compliance weight to 100 percent so that it dominates every other criterion
Qualitative criteria such as compliance cannot appear in any matrix, so it should be removed

rubric: Must-have conditions belong in a screen because compensatory scoring lets other strengths mask a disqualifier.
Distractors wrongly ban qualitative criteria or make the matrix meaningless by giving one criterion all the weight.

items.prompt: Five managers must choose a launch date within one hour. In earlier meetings the most senior manager spoke first and the others agreed. The criteria are to limit anchoring on her view and still finish within the hour. Which process is best?

options.label: Open the floor for discussion, then vote by show of hands so that every view counts equally
Run several rounds of talk with the senior manager opening each, to build agreement gradually
Have each person write a date and reasoning privately, reveal them together, then discuss the gaps
Appoint a devil's advocate to oppose whatever the senior manager says first, then decide together

rubric: Independent written estimates prevent anchoring and discussing the gaps fits the time limit.
Distractors still let the senior view shape early opinions, or vote after exposure to it.

items.prompt: A weighted decision matrix puts Vendor A at 3.92 and Vendor B at 3.85 out of 5. The weights came from one workshop and were never tested. Which next step best judges whether A should be chosen?

options.label: Add several more criteria until the gap between the vendors widens
Vary the weights within plausible ranges to see if the ranking flips
Accept Vendor A, since the matrix gives a clear numerical ranking and the weights were agreed in a workshop
Average the two vendors' scores to find a compromise between them

rubric: A 0.07 gap is within the noise of subjective weights, so sensitivity analysis shows how robust the ranking is.
Distractors treat spurious numeric precision as evidence or try to manufacture a gap.

items.prompt: A founder can take a one-off deal with a 60% chance of tripling the company's cash and a 40% chance of bankruptcy. Expected value is clearly positive. Which judgement best fits the criterion that the company must survive?

options.label: Take it, because a positive expected value means the deal wins on average
Reject it, because any option with a possible loss has negative value
Take it only if the team votes unanimously, because consensus removes the risk
Reject it as the sole rule, because ruin is absorbing and the bet can't be repeated

rubric: Expected value assumes many repetitions; with a non-repeatable ruinous outcome, survival dominates the average.
Distractors apply EV blindly, treat consensus as risk reduction, or reject all risk.

items.prompt: A pre-mortem is held after the CEO has announced she is committed to the plan. She opens the session, speaks first and the group brainstorms aloud. Which critique of the process is most valid?

options.label: The session is too short to surface real risks, since pre-mortems only work when run over several days of staged workshops
Failure stories should be limited to external risks such as market shifts, so that no individual or team is blamed for the plan
Authority and speaking order will suppress dissent, so failures should be imagined and written independently first
The method is flawed, because asking people to imagine failure makes teams pessimistic and lowers their commitment to the plan

rubric: Pre-mortems rely on licence to dissent; leader-first, spoken input produces conformity and anchoring.
Distractors misidentify the problem as duration, scope or the method's pessimism.

items.prompt: Launching a product has a 40% chance of +400k and a 60% chance of -200k; not launching yields 0. A consultancy offers a study costing 150k that it says will remove all uncertainty. Judge the offer.

options.label: Buy it, since removing all uncertainty is worth more than any fee
Decline it, because perfect information is worth at most 120k here
Buy it, because perfect information is worth 160k, the EV with the study, which exceeds the fee
Decline it, because information has no value when the launch EV is positive

rubric: Launch EV is 40k; with perfect information EV is 160k, so the ceiling on value is 120k, below the 150k fee.
Distractors misstate launch EV or claim information is either always or never valuable.

items.prompt: A project has consumed 2M. Finishing needs 1M more and would return about 0.8M, while redeploying the 1M elsewhere would return about 1.3M. Which reasoning is the soundest?

options.label: Finish, because stopping a project after heavy spending damages team morale
Finish, because abandoning now would waste the 2M already invested
Stop, because the 2M already lost shows the team can't deliver
Stop, because only future costs and returns matter and the alternative is better

rubric: Past spend is common to both options; comparing 0.8M against 1.3M on the same 1M favours redeployment.
Distractors reflect sunk-cost, morale and inference-from-past-failure fallacies.

items.prompt: A manager reviews a past hiring decision to judge its quality, separate from how the hire turned out. Which criteria are legitimate for judging the decision itself? Select all that apply.

options.label: Whether the decision was reached quickly with no disagreement
Whether the hire later performed well
Whether the criteria and trade-offs were stated before candidates were compared
Whether realistic alternatives were considered and the choice framed correctly
Whether the evidence gathered was reasonable for the stakes and time available

rubric: Decision quality rests on framing, information and explicit values at decision time.
Outcome and speed or consensus are poor proxies because luck and groupthink affect them.

items.prompt: A hiring panel scores candidates on a weighted matrix with criteria 'years of experience' (25%), 'seniority of previous titles' (25%), 'technical test' (30%) and 'communication' (20%). Experience and titles are strongly correlated. The leading candidate won mainly on those two. What is the most serious flaw in this design?

options.label: Communication has the lowest weight, so it can never change the final ranking of candidates
The technical test carries the highest single weight, so it dominates every other criterion in the ranking
Two correlated criteria count one trait at 50%, overweighting it relative to intent
Weights are fixed before scoring, so the panel cannot adjust them once a leading candidate emerges

rubric: Correlated criteria double count a single underlying trait and distort the intended weights.
Distractors confuse a legitimate top weight, a low weight or a normal sum with a design flaw.

items.prompt: You must design a hiring process that reduces noise between interviewers, keeps experienced judgement, and leaves an auditable trail. Which design meets all three constraints?

options.label: Panel discusses each candidate openly first, then each member records a final score, and the most senior member breaks any ties
A formula using only test score and years of experience ranks candidates, and the panel signs off on the ranking without discussion
Each interviewer scores set criteria independently, scores are aggregated, then the panel discusses gaps and decides
Interviewers form overall impressions, then vote by secret ballot, and the vote tally is filed as the record of the decision

rubric: Independent criterion-level scoring reduces noise, discussion retains judgement, and scores form the audit trail.
Distractors drop independence, drop judgement, or leave no criterion-level record.

items.prompt: Design a plan for an irreversible-looking expansion where capital is limited, leading indicators arrive within six months, and the firm must be able to stop without crippling losses. Which plan meets every constraint?

options.label: Split the budget equally across three unrelated markets at once, so that no single market failure can sink the firm
Run a funded pilot first, with kill and scale thresholds on early signals set before it starts
Delay all action for a year until the market is fully understood, then commit the whole budget in one step
Commit the full budget now to lock in the best terms, and rely on contingency reserves if results disappoint

rubric: Staged commitment with pre-set thresholds buys information, caps loss and preserves the option to stop.
Distractors commit fully, wait for certainty that never comes, or diversify without learning.

items.prompt: Design a 30-minute pre-mortem for eight people, one of them a dominant executive, that must surface varied failure modes and end with action. Which design satisfies all of this?

options.label: The executive opens by listing the likely failures, then others add to the list in turn, and the group assigns owners to the items on it
Each person silently writes failure stories, then they are collected, clustered and the top clusters get owners and mitigations
The team votes anonymously on whether the plan will fail, then discusses the main reasons given and proceeds only if most say no
Everyone discusses openly for 25 minutes, then the facilitator picks the top risks and writes up mitigations for the team afterward

rubric: Silent writing prevents anchoring on the executive, clustering shows variety, and owners create action.
Distractors keep authority-led anchoring, leave no action step, or replace failure stories with a vote.

items.prompt: A treasury team disagrees on whether a currency will fall, and discussions are anchored on the CFO's first guess. Design a hedging process that avoids anchoring, fixes action in advance and lets the team learn. Which design fits?

options.label: Collect independent probability estimates, aggregate them, set hedge triggers in advance and score forecasts later
The CFO states a view first, then the team debates in an open meeting until everyone agrees on one probability and the hedge ratio
Hire an outside forecaster, follow its call on each hedge decision and review the choice only when losses occur
Hedge a fixed 50% permanently so no forecast is needed, and revisit that ratio only when the board asks for it

rubric: Independent estimates avoid anchoring, advance triggers fix action and later scoring enables learning.
Distractors anchor on authority, drop forecasting entirely, or review only after bad outcomes.

items.prompt: A site-selection plan uses a weighted matrix plus a three-year NPV on the base-case demand forecast. The board requires the choice to be robust if demand is 30% below forecast. What is the plan missing?

options.label: A single blended score that merges the matrix and NPV into one number, so the board no longer has to reconcile two rankings that may disagree
A fourth matrix criterion for staff preferences, weighted enough to build buy-in and reduce resistance to whichever site is finally chosen
A low-demand stress test of rankings and NPV, plus a stated rule for what the board does if the leader changes
A longer NPV horizon that extends the forecast to ten years, since extra years smooth out demand uncertainty in the ranking

rubric: The robustness requirement needs scenario testing of the ranking and a pre-agreed response if it flips.
Distractors add preference, assume longer horizons fix uncertainty, or hide the conflict in one score.

items.prompt: You are drafting a charter for a recurring high-stakes decision. It must give clear ownership, allow later learning, and keep decision quality distinct from outcome luck. Which elements belong? Select all that apply.

options.label: A rule that the most senior attendee may veto any option
A named owner with decision criteria agreed up front
Permission to revise the criteria after results arrive so they match what worked
A scheduled review comparing outcomes with the original forecasts
A record of options, probabilities and rationale written before the outcome is known

rubric: Pre-outcome records, named ownership with up-front criteria and forecast review support accountability and learning.
Seniority vetoes and retrofitting criteria undermine both.

items.prompt: Two suppliers tie on your decision matrix, and the choice is due Friday. Delay costs about 20k per week, a wrong choice costs under 5k, and the contract can be exited with 30 days' notice. Which plan best meets these constraints?

options.label: Commission a four-week analysis of both suppliers to break the tie, accepting the delay as the price of greater certainty
Choose the supplier with easier exit terms now, and set a 60-day review against stated measures
Flip a coin and sign a three-year contract with the winner to lock in a volume discount
Split the order between both suppliers permanently so that the tie never has to be resolved

rubric: With cheap, reversible errors and costly delay, decide now, favour reversibility and build in a review.
Distractors overspend on analysis, lock in irreversibly, or avoid the decision structurally.
